title: Optimal binary search tree: plain recursion vs cubic DP vs Knuth's quadratic DP
problem_statement: Given keys k_1 < ... < k_n with non-negative integer access frequencies p_1, ..., p_n and non-negative integer gap frequencies q_0, ..., q_n (q_j counts searches for values strictly between k_j and k_(j+1), with k_0 = -infinity and k_(n+1) = +infinity), compute the minimum, over all binary search trees on k_1, ..., k_n, of sum_{m=1..n} p_m (level(k_m) + 1) + sum_{j=0..n} q_j level(gap j), where the root has level 0 and gap j is the external node (empty subtree) between k_j and k_(j+1). This is Knuth's (1971) cost: the weighted number of key comparisons over successful and unsuccessful searches. The output is that minimum as an exact integer (n = 0 gives 0).

input.size_measure: 2n + 1 non-negative integers (p_1..p_n, q_0..q_n). Complexities count arithmetic operations and comparisons on cost values as unit cost; all costs are at most (n + 1) times the total frequency, so they need only O(log n) more bits than the input numbers.

algorithms.name: plain recursion
algorithms.idea: c(i, j) = w(i, j) + min over roots k of c(i, k-1) + c(k, j), evaluated top-down without memoisation, so the Theta(n^2) subproblems are solved again and again.
algorithms.pseudocode: cost(i, j): if i = j return 0; return w(i, j) + min over i < k <= j of (cost(i, k-1) + cost(k, j)), with w(i, j) = q_i + sum_{m=i+1..j} (p_m + q_m); answer cost(0, n)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(3^n) on every input: exactly 3^n calls and (3^(n-1) - 1)/2 cost comparisons for n >= 1
algorithms.correctness: Optimal substructure: the subtrees of an optimal tree's root k are optimal for (i, k-1) and (k, j), and the cost of a tree is w(i, j) plus the costs of its two subtrees (every node's level grows by one under the root). Count: calls K(m) = 1 + 2 sum_{t<m} K(t), K(0) = 1, so K(m) = 3 K(m-1) = 3^m; comparisons C(m) = (m-1) + 2 sum_{t<m} C(t), C(0) = 0, so C(m) = 3 C(m-1) + 1 (m >= 2), C(1) = 0, i.e. C(m) = (3^(m-1) - 1)/2. Both confirmed by exact counts for n = 0..11.

algorithms.name: cubic interval DP (every root)
algorithms.idea: Fill c[i][j] for increasing length j - i; every interval tries every one of its roots.
algorithms.pseudocode: c[i][i] = 0; for L = 1..n, for i = 0..n-L: j = i + L; w[i][j] = w[i][j-1] + p_j + q_j; c[i][j] = w[i][j] + min over i < k <= j of (c[i][k-1] + c[k][j]); return c[0][n]
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^3) on every input: n(n+1)(n+2)/6 candidate roots, (n+1)n(n-1)/6 cost comparisons
algorithms.correctness: The same recurrence evaluated bottom-up; each interval's subintervals are shorter and already filled (Knuth 1971; textbook DP, e.g. CLRS, Section 15.5 in the 3rd edition). An interval of length L makes L - 1 comparisons, and sum_{L=1..n} (n - L + 1)(L - 1) = C(n+1, 3).

algorithms.name: Knuth's speed-up (monotone roots)
algorithms.idea: Same recurrence, but the root of (i, j) is searched only between r[i][j-1] and r[i+1][j], the roots chosen for the two intervals one shorter; the implementation keeps the largest minimiser in the range.
algorithms.pseudocode: as the cubic DP, but for j - i >= 2 the min runs over r[i][j-1] <= k <= r[i+1][j] (r[i][i+1] = i + 1), and r[i][j] = the largest k attaining the min
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) on every input. Upper bound: for each length L >= 2 the range widths telescope, sum_i (r[i+1][i+L] - r[i][i+L-1] + 1) = (n - L + 1) + r[n-L+1][n] - r[0][L-1] <= 2n - L; lower bound: n(n+1)/2 intervals, each doing at least one candidate. Exactly sum_{L=2..n} (r[n-L+1][n] - r[0][L-1]) <= (n-1)^2 cost comparisons, with equality on the V2 family (two heavy end keys).
algorithms.correctness: With non-negative frequencies, w(i, j) is an interval sum, so it satisfies the quadrangle inequality (with equality) and is monotone under interval inclusion; then c satisfies the quadrangle inequality and the optimal roots can be chosen monotone, r[i][j-1] <= r[i][j] <= r[i+1][j] (Knuth 1971 for optimum BSTs; Yao 1980 for the general quadrangle-inequality recurrence; statements as commonly cited, texts not re-read here). Ties (derivation, ours, consistent with the experiment): if every chosen root lies in its range, r[i][j-1] <= r[i+1][j-1] <= r[i+1][j] by induction, so no range is empty; and the quadrangle inequality of c gives c_k'(i, j) <= c_k(i, j) for ANY optimal root k' of (i, j-1) and every k < k' (symmetrically at the upper end), so the range contains an optimal root of (i, j) whatever minimiser was kept before. experiments/2026-10-07b_optimal_bst_ties.py confirms: largest, smallest, random and two deliberately inconsistent tie rules give the correct value on 6006 tie-heavy instances.

relationship: Plain recursion over the root is exponential, Theta(3^n), because it recomputes the Theta(n^2) interval subproblems; memoising them gives the Theta(n^3) DP (the T2 step). Knuth's monotone-root restriction makes the DP's root searches telescope to Theta(n^2) in total (the T3 step). Exact comparison counts: (3^(n-1) - 1)/2, (n+1)n(n-1)/6 and at most (n-1)^2.

sources.title: Efficient dynamic programming using quadrangle inequalities
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 12th Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 1980), 429-435
sources.note: Generalises Knuth's speed-up: if w satisfies the quadrangle inequality and is monotone on intervals, the recurrence c(i, j) = w(i, j) + min_k (c(i, k-1) + c(k, j)) can be solved in O(n^2). Statement as commonly cited; the text was not re-read for this entry.

sources.authors: Cormen, T. H.; Leiserson, C. E.; Rivest, R. L.; Stein, C.
sources.title: Introduction to Algorithms (3rd ed.)
sources.note: Section 15.5: optimal binary search trees and the Theta(n^3) DP; its cost counts every external node at level + 1, i.e. adds sum q_j to Knuth's cost (section number as recalled, not re-checked here).

verification.method: V1: the three implementations agree with each other and with an independent oracle in harness.py: for n <= 10 it enumerates every BST shape explicitly (Catalan(n) shapes) and computes the cost from the level of every key and gap, with no interval recurrence; for 10 < n <= 60 it uses a separately written memoised recursion with prefix sums (same recurrence, independent code). Battery: n = 0..10, 13, 20, 40, 70, 100 with 12 instances per n drawn from ten families, most of them full of ties (frequencies in {0, 1}, in [0, 3], all zero, all equal, gaps only, keys only), plus wide random weights, one heavy key, geometric weights and two heavy end keys; plain recursion up to n = 10. Of the 192 instances, 132 (n <= 10) are checked by the shape enumeration, 36 (n = 13..40) by the memoised recursion, and 24 (n = 70, 100) only by agreement of the two DPs; a wrong value (output + 1) is rejected on all 156 checked instances with n >= 1 (part3 of experiments/2026-10-07b_optimal_bst_ties.py). experiments/2026-10-07b_optimal_bst_ties.py adds 6006 tie-heavy instances (n = 2..14) on which Knuth's algorithm with five tie rules matches the cubic DP. V2 (measure 'reported'): the exact number of COMPARISONS of two cost values made by the unchanged implementations, counted by the harness's CountingInt number type, on the two-heavy-end-keys family (Knuth's worst case). Exact counts: recursion (3^(n-1) - 1)/2 (n = 5..11), cubic DP (n+1)n(n-1)/6 (n = 16..128), Knuth (n-1)^2 (n = 32..512); each closed form is proven (see correctness) and checked value by value in experiments/2026-10-07b_optimal_bst_counts.py. Fits at tolerance 0.04: alpha = 1.002 (3^n), 1.001 (n^3), 1.010 (n^2). Rivals rejected: recursion vs 2^n 1.587, 4^n 0.794, Catalan-like 4^n/n^1.5 0.923; cubic DP vs n^2 1.501, n^4 0.750; Knuth vs n^3 0.674, n 2.021, n log n 1.668, n^2 log n 0.914. On seven other families (random small, wide, one heavy key, geometric, all zero, gaps only, keys only) Knuth's counts lie between 0.39 n^2 and 0.61 n^2 for n = 32..512, with alpha against n^2 from 0.993 to 1.013 (same script), so the tolerance covers them too.

caveats: The Theta(n^2) of Knuth's algorithm relies on non-negative frequencies (w monotone and satisfying the quadrangle inequality). Tie-breaking among the minimisers inside Knuth's range does not matter (see the correctness note and the ties experiment), but monotonicity is NOT a property of arbitrary optimal roots: a table that takes the largest optimal root for even i and the smallest for odd i from the full optimal sets is non-monotone on 3417 of 6006 tie-heavy instances (e.g. all-zero weights, n >= 4). CLRS's cost differs from Knuth's by the constant sum_j q_j (CLRS counts an external node at level + 1), which does not change the optimal trees. Counts measure comparisons of cost values only; additions are also Theta(3^n), Theta(n^3) and Theta(n^2) (exact values read off the data in the counts experiment: (35 * 3^(n-2) - 3)/2 for the recursion, n >= 2; n(n+1)(n+2)/6 + 3n(n+1)/2 - n for the cubic DP; comparisons + 2n^2 for Knuth), and index arithmetic is not counted. The plain recursion recomputes w(i, j) by summation in every call; this does not change Theta(3^n).
notes: Introduces the 'monotone root / quadrangle inequality' speed-up family (Knuth-Yao) to the dataset. The pattern report (research/2026-10-07_patterns.md, candidate 6) estimated Theta(3^n) for the plain recursion by analogy with matrix chain; exact call counts confirm it: 3^n calls exactly (the recursion also calls itself on empty intervals), and (3^(n-1) - 1)/2 comparisons.
